title: Manual or AI Data Entry for Historic Club Records?
description: A practical comparison of manual transcription, OCR and AI-assisted review for historic sports club trophy records, with a pilot evaluation checklist.
html:
A club’s membership administration and its historical archive are different jobs. Membership software may manage current subscriptions and bookings. A trophy archive needs to recover names and dates from old sources, preserve uncertainty and make reviewed winners searchable. Start by naming the problem you want to solve.

Three approaches to entering historical records

Manual transcription means a person reads the original source and enters the information. It can be a sensible choice for a short, legible list or where the reviewer already understands difficult initials. It still needs proofreading and a clear record of the source.

Ordinary OCR, or optical character recognition, reads text from an image. It can be useful for clear printed material. Engraved metal creates different challenges: shallow lettering, reflection, curvature and wear. Try the actual source rather than assuming that a tool which reads a letter will read a polished cup equally well.

AI-assisted transcription proposes readings from the photographs you provide. In Trophy Guru, the club reviews and edits those proposed names and years. An apparently plausible name can still be wrong, so the output is a draft for checking, not an official historical record.

Compare the whole workflow

Timing only the automatic reading gives an incomplete picture. Include gathering the source, taking photographs, uploading images, checking the output, finding other evidence and exporting the result. A worn inscription may require more historical research than typing, whichever method you choose.

  • Choose a representative trophy with both clear and difficult entries.
  • Record the number of readable names and the entries that remain ambiguous.
  • Time capture, entry and review separately.
  • Count corrections to names and years, not just the number of rows produced.
  • Check whether the final list can be traced back to the source.
  • Compare the result against the same carefully reviewed reference list.

A small pilot tells you something about your sources. It does not establish a universal accuracy rate, and a neat-looking output should not be treated as proof of correctness. We do not claim that human review guarantees 100% accuracy or that an AI system cannot make repeated mistakes.

Use people where interpretation matters

An inscription such as “J. Smith” may refer to more than one person. A membership list can suggest candidates, but it cannot by itself establish who won a competition decades earlier. Consult result sheets, honours books, minutes or other club evidence. Leave the identity unresolved until the evidence supports it.

Similarly, an empty year is a gap in the current archive. It may reflect a missing plate, an unreadable entry or a competition that was not held. These are different historical explanations. Avoid filling a gap with a guess simply to make the list complete.

What Trophy Guru automates

Trophy Guru proposes winner records from an uploaded set of trophy and source photographs. The club can edit names and years, add missing winners from other evidence, confirm records, export CSV data and publish an online honours board. It is not a replacement for membership billing, pitch bookings or competition scoring software.

The useful test is whether the service helps your club produce checked records from its own collection. Use the same source material and review standard when comparing different approaches.
